pathogen_scientific_name.value: Barley yellow dwarf virus (BYDV) — multiple species in family Luteoviridae
pathogen_scientific_name.quote: Barley yellow dwarf virus (BYDV), a member of the Luteoviruses, is a group of five closely related virus strains.

type_of_disease.quote: The disease is caused by at least eight viral species that belongs to the Luteoviridae virus family, and it is transmitted by aphids.

affected_parts.quote: Symptoms generally appear first on the older leaves of young plants as faint yellowish-green blotches near the leaf tip. Plants infected early (in the fall) are usually dwarfed and yield much less than plants infected at a later stage of development.

summary.value: Yellowing, reddening, or purpling of leaf tips progressing to full leaves, with plant dwarfing in early infections. Leaves may become stiff and erect with inward-rolling necrotic margins. Affected plants appear singly or in small patches among normal plants.
summary.quote: The blotches enlarge rapidly and merge, changing to shades of red to purple in oats, yellow to red in wheat and bright yellow in barley. The leaves may lose their flexuous appearance and become erect or stiff. The leaf margin near the tip may roll inward and become necrotic forming a stiff point.

diagnostic_features.value: Reddish-purple or yellowish discoloration of the flag leaf; yellowing patches visible in fields often in circular patterns; color varies by host: red to purple in oats, yellow to red in wheat, bright yellow in barley. Does not produce a distinct mosaic pattern. Pale yellowing of older leaf tips is typical; during cool temperatures the tips can become reddish-purple.
diagnostic_features.quote: Reddish-purple or yellowish discoloration of the flag leaf is the most characteristic symptoms of BYDV. In Ohio, it is rare to see entire fields affected, but most frequently BYDV occurs on scattered plants or in circular patches within fields.

look_alikes.quote: Early symptoms of BYDV are frequently overlooked because infected plants resemble those with mineral deficiencies, low temperature damage, root rots, herbicide injury, or other problems.

conflicts.canonical_value: at least eight viral species in family Luteoviridae
conflicts.alternative_value: a group of five closely related virus strains (Luteoviruses)
conflicts.note: OSU extension states 'at least eight viral species'; UNL CropWatch states 'five closely related virus strains'. OSU is more recent and more specific; UNL may reflect older taxonomy.

pathogen_scientific_name.quote: Cephalosporium stripe is caused by the fungus Cephalosporium gramineum

type_of_disease.quote: Cephalosporium stripe is caused by the fungus Cephalosporium gramineum

affected_parts.quote: Stripes appear in leaves at any growth stage; Note the necrotic areas on the stems; Plants are infected through wounds in the root system; this fungus attacks the vascular system; heads either are empty or are filled with shriveled kernels

summary.value: Yellow stripes running from the tip of the leaf blade to its base and down the leaf sheath, with brown necrotic streaks developing in the center of the stripes as leaves age. Infected stems are stunted causing a double-canopy of healthy and infected heads. Severely infected stems die prematurely resulting in dull-colored whiteheads containing only shriveled grain.
summary.quote: Yellow stripes running from the tip of the leaf blade to its base and down the leaf sheath is characteristic of Cephalosporium stripe. Each leaf may have one to three stripes. As leaves age, fine, brown (necrotic) streaks develop in the center of the stripes and extend down the leaf sheaths. ... Infected stems are stunted leading to a double-canopy of healthy and infected heads. Severely infected stems die prematurely, resulting in dead, standing stems, or whiteheads. Color of the whiteheads is usually dull and not typical of healthy, bright-colored straw.

diagnostic_features.value: Distinct yellow stripes (one to three per leaf) extending the full length of the leaf blade and down the leaf sheath, with brown necrotic streaks in the center representing colonized xylem tissue. Vascular bundles are brown within the yellow stripes along affected leaf sheaths and joints are darkened inside. Whiteheads are dull-colored rather than bright straw-colored. No powdery spores present in the stripes.
diagnostic_features.quote: Yellow stripes running from the tip of the leaf blade to its base and down the leaf sheath is characteristic of Cephalosporium stripe. Each leaf may have one to three stripes. As leaves age, fine, brown (necrotic) streaks develop in the center of the stripes and extend down the leaf sheaths. These streaks are the colonized water-conducting tissue (xylem) that becomes plugged with the fungus. ... Color of the whiteheads is usually dull and not typical of healthy, bright-colored straw.

look_alikes.quote: Stripe rust may be confused with Cephalosporium stripe; however, the stripes are shorter and do not extend the length of the leaf blade and down the leaf sheath. Stripe rust lesions usually have powdery, yellow-orange-colored spores on the leaf that can be wiped-off with a finger.

conflicts.note: PNW Handbooks notes the sexual stage name as Hymenula cerealis: 'The soilborne fungus, Cephalosporium gramineum (sexual: Hymenula cerealis)'. No taxonomy validation was available to confirm current accepted name.

conflicts.alternative_value: Foliar, Stem, Vascular (no Root or Seed listed)
conflicts.note: CPN and WSU list Foliar/Stem/Vascular; PNW Handbooks additionally specifies Root infection and Seed (shriveled kernels). The broader list from PNW Handbooks is used as canonical.

pathogen_scientific_name.quote: Two fungi, Tilletia tritici (syn. = T. caries ) and T. laevis (syn. = T. foetida )

type_of_disease.quote: Two fungi, Tilletia tritici (syn. = T. caries ) and T. laevis (syn. = T. foetida )

affected_parts.quote: In infected heads, light brown smut balls filled with dark brown spore masses replace all or part of the kernels. Bunted heads remain green longer, and plants may be slightly stunted, and glumes can be distorted.

summary.value: Spikelets develop off-green discoloration and appear greasy as heads ripen. Glumes open as if overstuffed as large spore masses (bunt balls) form within spikelets, eventually rupturing the seed coat to reveal large masses of black spores. Light brown smut balls filled with dark brown spore masses replace kernels in infected heads, releasing a distinctive foul fishy odor when crushed. Plants may be slightly stunted with distorted glumes and heads that remain green longer.
summary.quote: As heads ripen (FGS 10.5.3), spikelets may develop an off-green discoloration and appear greasy. Glumes start to open as if "overstuffed" as large spore masses (bunt balls) form within spikelets. Bunt balls grow within the seed coat, which becomes fragile and eventually ruptures to reveal large masses of black spores.

diagnostic_features.value: Bunt balls roughly the shape of a wheat kernel (not globular) with black spores and a distinct fishy odor; no positive symptoms apparent until the crop heads; infected heads thinner and remain green longer; awns of infected heads may be smaller or completely missing; plants not severely stunted.
diagnostic_features.quote: Wheat with common bunt will not be severely stunted, and bunt balls will be roughly the shape of a wheat kernel, not globular. Spores give off a distinct fishy odor. In awned varieties, awns of infected heads may be smaller or are completely missing. Infected heads tend to be thinner and may not lose green coloration as quickly.

conflicts.canonical_value: Tilletia tritici (syn. T. caries) and T. laevis (syn. T. foetida)
conflicts.note: Crop Protection Network uses the synonym T. caries; PNW Handbooks lists T. tritici as the current name with T. caries as synonym. No taxonomy validation was provided; canonical value follows PNW Handbooks which explicitly notes the synonymy.
Crop Protection Network notes foliar symptoms (off-green discoloration of spikelets); PNW Handbooks emphasizes seed and whole plant. Both are included in the merged canonical value.

pathogen_scientific_name.quote: Dwarf bunt is a result of a soilborne pathogen ( Tilletia controversa) and the disease is also known as dwarf smut.

type_of_disease.quote: Fungal germination takes several weeks and is favored by moist conditions with soil temperatures between 37-46°F.

affected_parts.quote: Symptoms prior to heading (FGS 10.5) include yellow leaf flecking at late seedling stage, stunting, and excessive tillering. Once the head emerges, the fungus transforms kernels into spherical bunt balls.

summary.value: Infected plants are stunted with excessive tillering and yellow leaf flecking at late seedling stage. Once heads emerge, kernels are transformed into spherical bunt balls filled with dark colored spores having a fishy odor. Infected heads maintain green color longer, with noticeably splayed spikes and awns.
summary.quote: Symptoms prior to heading (FGS 10.5) include yellow leaf flecking at late seedling stage, stunting, and excessive tillering. Once the head emerges, the fungus transforms kernels into spherical bunt balls. Infected heads may maintain green color longer, and spikes and awns will be noticeably splayed. Bunt balls are filled with dark colored spores having a fishy odor.

diagnostic_features.value: Spherical bunt balls (distinguishing from common bunt's kernel-shaped balls) in heads with a characteristic fishy odor; plant stunting notably dwarfed compared to healthy plants; smut balls emit a distinctive foul odor when crushed.
diagnostic_features.quote: Infected plants are dwarfed compared to healthy plants. Smut balls containing masses of dark smut spores replace kernels. If crushed, a smut ball emits a distinctive foul odor as in common bunt.

look_alikes.quote: Bunt balls will be present with dwarf bunt, which can help distinguish the disease from abiotic disorders such as nutrient deficiencies, chemical injury, and soil compaction. Related Resources Loose Smut of Wheat Common Bunt of Wheat

pathogen_scientific_name.quote: we will refer to Oculimacula yallundae and Oculimacula acuformis as the causal agents of eyespot of wheat. Both species can co-exist within the same field, cause identical symptoms on wheat, and follow the same disease cycle.

type_of_disease.quote: Eyespot of Wheat: How to identify and control this common fungal disease

affected_parts.quote: a lower stem-infecting foot rot pathogen ... Infection results in characteristic elliptical or eye-shaped lesions on the lower stem ... the lesion will penetrate the stem tissue ... Lesions can also girdle the flow of water and nutrients to the ripening wheat head

summary.value: Characteristic elliptical or eye-shaped lesions on the lower stem with a dark brown perimeter and yellowish-brown center; severe infections show whitish-gray mycelium inside the hollow stem and may cause multidirectional lodging and premature white heads.
summary.quote: Infection results in characteristic elliptical or eye-shaped lesions on the lower stem (Figure 2A). Lesions typically have a dark brown perimeter that distinguishes between healthy and infected tissue (Figure 2B). The center of each lesion is typically yellowish-brown and may have dark brown-blackish pseudoparenchyma fruiting bodies (Figure 2B). In severe infections, the lesion will penetrate the stem tissue, and a whitish-gray mass of fungus, called mycelium, may be visible inside the hollow wheat stem (Figure 2C).

diagnostic_features.value: Elliptical (eye-shaped) lesions on the lower stem with a dark brown perimeter separating healthy and infected tissue; yellowish-brown lesion center with dark brown-blackish pseudoparenchyma fruiting bodies; whitish-gray mycelium visible inside the hollow stem in severe infections; brittle lesion tissue causing multidirectional lodging; lodged stems break off at soil line when pulled.
diagnostic_features.quote: Lesions typically have a dark brown perimeter that distinguishes between healthy and infected tissue (Figure 2B). The center of each lesion is typically yellowish-brown and may have dark brown-blackish pseudoparenchyma fruiting bodies (Figure 2B). In severe infections, the lesion will penetrate the stem tissue, and a whitish-gray mass of fungus, called mycelium, may be visible inside the hollow wheat stem (Figure 2C). Eyespot lesions are brittle in contrast to surrounding healthy tissue and thus weaken the stem (Figure 1), which may result in multidirectional lodging

look_alikes.quote: What eyespot is not : Rhizoctonia cerealis, the causal agent of sharp eyespot of wheat.

conflicts.note: WSU states 'Eyespot only affects stems; roots are not colonized.' OSU extension additionally identifies vascular/nutrient-flow girding.

pathogen_scientific_name.quote: Fusarium root, crown, and foot rot is caused by several Fusarium spp.

type_of_disease.quote: all soilborne fungi that live on old stubble and straw in the soil

affected_parts.quote: dark brown lesions on primary and secondary roots. A dark brown to red lesion will be apparent near the first node of the wheat plant. Pink, cottony fungal growth may be evident inside lower portions of infected stems. If heads survive, seed will likely be shriveled.

summary.value: Brown discoloration of roots and subcrown internode progressing to dark brown at boot stage; dark brown to red lesion near the first node; pink cottony fungal growth inside lower stems; premature white heads with shriveled or absent kernels.
summary.quote: Root, crown, and foot rot symptoms include dark brown lesions on primary and secondary roots. A dark brown to red lesion will be apparent near the first node of the wheat plant. Infected plants may die prematurely, resulting in white heads. If heads survive, seed will likely be shriveled.

diagnostic_features.value: Dark brown to red lesion near the first node; pink, cottony fungal growth inside lower stems; infected crowns spongy and heavily decayed under humid conditions; infected seedlings reddish with poor vigor and poor tiller production; lower stem above first node streaked or uniformly brown.
diagnostic_features.quote: A dark brown to red lesion will be apparent near the first node of the wheat plant. Under humid conditions, the interior of infected crowns will be spongy and heavily decayed. Pink, cottony fungal growth may be evident inside lower portions of infected stems. Infected seedlings tend to be reddish with poor vigor and poor tiller production.

look_alikes.quote: Wheat ( Triticum aestivum ) - Common Root Rot (Seedling Blight) Wheat ( Triticum aestivum ) - Eyespot (Strawbreaker Foot Rot)

pathogen_scientific_name.quote: Rhizoctonia cerealis, the causal agent of sharp eyespot of wheat.
Parastagonospora nodorum (syn.Septoria nodorum) is a fungal pathogen

type_of_disease.quote: Parastagonospora nodorum (syn.Septoria nodorum) is a fungal pathogen

affected_parts.quote: can produce symptoms on leaves, stems, glumes, and awns

summary.value: Small yellow spots that enlarge into oval or 'cat eye' shaped lesions with dark-brown centers on leaves; infected glumes appear dirty from a distance and are purple to brown in color.
summary.quote: Symptoms begin in the low canopy as small, yellow spots. Over time these lesions enlarge into an oval or "cat eye" shape with a dark-brown center (Fig 1). Under favorable conditions, the entire leaf blade may become covered with lesions greatly reducing photosynthetic ability. Infected glumes may look dirty from a distance and are purple to brown in color (Fig 2).

diagnostic_features.value: Oval or 'cat eye' shaped lesions with dark-brown centers on leaves; glumes that appear dirty and are purple to brown in color.
diagnostic_features.quote: these lesions enlarge into an oval or "cat eye" shape with a dark-brown center (Fig 1). Infected glumes may look dirty from a distance and are purple to brown in color (Fig 2).

pathogen_scientific_name.quote: Damage is caused by the fungus Alternaria triticina.

type_of_disease.quote: Alternaria triticina Fungus

affected_parts.quote: The lowermost leaves are always the first to show signs of infection, which gradually spreads to the upper leaves. ... In severe cases, leaf sheaths, awns and glumes are also affected and have a burnt appearance.

summary.value: Small, oval, chlorotic lesions irregularly scattered on leaves that enlarge into dark brown or grey sunken lesions, eventually merging and killing the entire leaf. In severe cases, leaf sheaths, awns and glumes have a burnt appearance.
summary.quote: Small, oval, discolored lesions can be found scattered on the leaves in an irregular manner. As the lesions enlarge, they become dark brown to grey and irregular in shape. The leaves eventually dry.

diagnostic_features.value: Lesions are oval and chlorotic initially, becoming irregular, dark brown or grey and sunken, with a bright yellow marginal zone, up to 1 cm or more in diameter. Under moist conditions, lesions may be covered by black powdery conidia. In severe cases, leaf sheaths, awns and glumes have a burnt appearance.
diagnostic_features.quote: Lesions may have a bright yellow marginal zone and can grow up to 1cm or more in diameter. Under moist conditions, lesions may be covered by black powdery conidia. At later stages of the disease, lesions will merge together resulting in the death of the entire leaf. In severe cases, leaf sheaths, awns and glumes are also affected and have a burnt appearance.

conflicts.canonical_value: Small, oval, chlorotic lesions irregularly scattered on leaves that enlarge into dark brown or grey sunken lesions, eventually merging and killing the entire leaf.
conflicts.alternative_value: Reddish brown oval spots appear on young seedlings with bright yellow margin. In severe cases, several spots coalesce to cause drying of leaves.
conflicts.note: eagri.org emphasises reddish-brown colour and seedling stage; Plantix describes broader disease progress across all leaves with dark brown/grey colour.

pathogen_scientific_name.quote: BLS is caused by the bacterium Xanthomonas translucens.

type_of_disease.quote: Bacterial streak, caused by Xanthomonas campestris pv. undulosa

affected_parts.quote: appears first as small water-soaked lesions that rapidly develop into long, thin, tan-brown, water-soaked lesions, confined between the leaf veins ... Black chaff symptoms are present on the peduncle, rachis, and glumes. Infected peduncle and rachis tissues are dark brown ... infected seed can spread the pathogen

summary.value: Small water-soaked lesions on leaves that develop into long, thin, tan-brown streaks confined between veins, with milky bacterial ooze that dries to a scale-like glaze; on heads, dark brown to black discoloration of the peduncle, rachis, and glumes (black chaff).
summary.quote: appears first as small water-soaked lesions that rapidly develop into long, thin, tan-brown, water-soaked lesions, confined between the leaf veins ... Black chaff symptoms are present on the peduncle, rachis, and glumes. Infected peduncle and rachis tissues are dark brown, dark purple, or black.

diagnostic_features.value: Lesions are translucent when backlit; milky droplets of bacterial ooze within lesions when free moisture is present; dried ooze gives a shiny or glazed appearance with small amber-colored granules; lesions confined between leaf veins; symptoms most evident on the middle third of the leaf blade; alternating bands of green and pigmented awn tissue in awned varieties; streaked lesions (not spotty or blotchy).
diagnostic_features.quote: Lesions may appear translucent when backlit, especially when leaves are wet ... The bacterium exudes milky droplets of bacterial ooze within lesions when free-moisture is present on leaves. The ooze will give the leaves a shiny or glazed appearance when dry and small, amber-colored granules of dried exudates may be evident in lesions. Symptoms are often most evident on the middle third of the leaf blade ... In awned varieties, alternating bands of green and pigmented awn tissue may be evident.

look_alikes.quote: BLS infection caused by Xanthomonas translucens shouldn't be confused with bacterial leaf blight (BLB) caused by Pseudomonas syringae ... This exudate is one way to distinguish BLS from a brown, black or purple discoloration of the glumes (melanosis) that's associated with a genetic syndrome called pseudo black chaff

conflicts.note: Crop Protection Network uses the older pathovar designation Xanthomonas campestris pv. undulosa; UMN Extension uses the current accepted name Xanthomonas translucens. No NCBI/MycoBank validation was available; UMN (higher-authority extension) name selected as canonical.

pathogen_scientific_name.quote: bacterial leaf blight (BLB) caused by Pseudomonas syringae

type_of_disease.quote: bacterial leaf blight (BLB) caused by Pseudomonas syringae

affected_parts.quote: causes spotty and blotchy leaf lesions

summary.value: Spotty and blotchy leaf lesions, in contrast to the streaked lesions of bacterial leaf streak.
summary.quote: causes spotty and blotchy leaf lesions rather than the streaked lesions of BLS

diagnostic_features.value: Spotty and blotchy leaf lesions rather than the long, thin, streaked lesions characteristic of bacterial leaf streak.
diagnostic_features.quote: causes spotty and blotchy leaf lesions rather than the streaked lesions of BLS

look_alikes.quote: BLS infection caused by Xanthomonas translucens shouldn't be confused with bacterial leaf blight (BLB)

pathogen_scientific_name.quote: In Ohio, the principal pathogen is Fusarium graminearum (the sexual stage is Gibberella zeae), but F. avenaceum (G. avenaceum) and F. culmorum (no known sexual state) have also been reported.

type_of_disease.quote: caused by the fungus Fusarium graminearum and related species

affected_parts.quote: Infected kernels are generally shrunken, wrinkled, and light-weight, with a rough, scabby appearance. When the fungus infects the stem immediately below the head the entire head may die.

summary.value: Diseased spikelets turn light-straw colored and bleached while healthy spikelets remain green. Infected kernels are shrunken, wrinkled, light-weight, and discolored, ranging from light-brown to pink to grayish white. Pink or orange spore masses can be observed on infected spikelets, particularly at the base.
summary.quote: Diseased spikelets turn light-straw colored and have a bleached appearance due to premature death of tissues. Healthy spikelets on the same head retain their normal green color. Infected kernels are generally shrunken, wrinkled, and light-weight, with a rough, scabby appearance. These kernels range in color from light-brown to pink to grayish white.

diagnostic_features.value: Pinkish to salmon-colored spore masses (sporodochia) form on the margin of the glumes near the base of the spikelet, best seen early in the morning before dew dries. Dark purplish-black fruiting bodies (perithecia) may appear on mature heads in cool, moist weather. Shriveled, chalky, white-pink discolored 'tombstone' kernels are lightweight and highly contaminated with mycotoxins.
diagnostic_features.quote: Within 7 to 10 days after symptom development pinkish to salmon-colored spore masses and mycelium (called sporodochia) may form on the margin of the glumes of individual spikelets, especially near the base of the spikelet. The pink spore masses are easiest to see early in the morning before the dew dries. Towards the end of the season, heads with diseased spikelets may become speckled with dark purplish-black fruiting bodies (perithecia) of the fungus if the weather remains cool and moist.

conflicts.note: CPN only lists Seed; OSU extension also identifies Stem as affected when fungus infects stem immediately below the head.

pathogen_scientific_name.quote: The Karnal bunt fungus ( Tilletia indica Mitra) and the plant disease it causes are harmless to people and animals

type_of_disease.quote: The Karnal bunt fungus ( Tilletia indica Mitra)

affected_parts.quote: The most conspicuous symptom is the presence of small numbers of harvested seeds containing tissue that is gray at first but later turns black.

summary.value: Harvested seeds contain tissue that is gray at first but later turns black, with discoloration often limited to the embryo end but sometimes extending over the entire kernel. In advanced infections kernels are blackened, sooty, and fragile, resembling a boat or dugout canoe shape, and may produce a strong fishy smell.
summary.quote: Bunted kernels are fragile, blackened, and sooty. The kernels' outer layer will have cracks, and if you press them, you'll see a black powder. In advanced infections, wheat kernels look like a boat or dugout canoe.

diagnostic_features.value: Blackened, sooty kernels with cracked outer layer revealing black powder when pressed; advanced infections produce a boat or dugout canoe shape; severe infections produce trimethylamine giving a strong fishy odor. Requires microscope and biochemical tests for accurate field identification.
diagnostic_features.quote: In advanced infections, wheat kernels look like a boat or dugout canoe. Fishy Odor If the disease is severe, kernels will produce trimethylamine, which gives off a strong, fishy smell.

conflicts.canonical_value: Blackened, sooty, fragile kernels with cracked outer layer; boat or dugout canoe shape in advanced infections; fishy odor in severe cases
conflicts.alternative_value: Gray to black discolored tissue limited to embryo end only but may extend over entire kernel
conflicts.note: PNW Handbooks emphasizes gray-to-black progression limited to embryo end; USDA APHIS describes more advanced blackened/sooty appearance with boat shape and fishy odor. Both descriptions are consistent with different disease stages.

pathogen_scientific_name.quote: SCIENTIFIC NAME: Puccinia graminis Pers.:Pers. f. sp. tritici Eriks. E. Henn.

type_of_disease.quote: SCIENTIFIC NAME: Puccinia graminis Pers.:Pers. f. sp. tritici Eriks. E. Henn.

affected_parts.quote: Uredinia generally appear as oval lesions on leaf sheaths, true stem, and spike. Uredinia can appear on the leaves if other diseases have not killed them.

summary.value: Pustules (uredinia) containing red to orange spores erupt from stem and leaf tissue; uredinia are brick red, oval, and rupture the host epidermis with infected areas rough to the touch. The emerging spores tear tissue giving pustules a characteristic tattered appearance.
summary.quote: Pustules containing red to orange spores erupt from stem and leaf tissue. The damage inflicted by the emerging spores tears leaf tissue, giving pustules a characteristic tattered appearance.

diagnostic_features.value: Brick red oval uredinia that rupture the epidermis, sporulating on both leaf surfaces, with infected areas rough to the touch. Spores are a deeper red color than leaf rust and stripe rust. Grain is shriveled due to damage to conducting tissue and severe disease can cause straw breakage. Pustules can also be found on glumes and awns.
diagnostic_features.quote: Uredinia are brick red in color and can be seen to rupture the host epidermis, on the leaves uredinia generally penetrate to sporulate on both surfaces. Infected areas are rough to the touch. Grain is shriveled due to the damage to the conducting tissue

look_alikes.quote: Spores of the stem rust pathogen tend to be a deeper red color than those observed with leaf rust and stripe rust.

conflicts.alternative_value: Puccinia graminis subsp. graminis and P. graminis f. sp. tritici
conflicts.note: Crop Protection Network lists both subspecies graminis and f. sp. tritici; USDA ARS lists only f. sp. tritici which is the accepted form for wheat stem rust.

pathogen_scientific_name.quote: Stripe rust of wheat is caused by the basidiomycete fungus Puccinia striiformis Westend f. sp. tritici Eriks & Henn

type_of_disease.quote: caused by the basidiomycete fungus Puccinia striiformis

affected_parts.quote: small, bright yellow, elongated uredial pustules arranged in conspicuous rows on the leaves, leaf sheaths, glumes and awns

summary.value: Yellow streaks (pre-pustules) followed by small, bright yellow, elongated uredial pustules arranged in conspicuous rows (stripes) on leaves, leaf sheaths, glumes and awns. Small yellowish uredinia appear in linear rows on the leaf; a single infection can result in a stripe the length of the leaf. Stunting of plants is common with severe early infections.
summary.quote: The first sign of stripe rust is the appearance of yellow streaks (pre-pustules), followed by small, bright yellow, elongated uredial pustules arranged in conspicuous rows on the leaves, leaf sheaths, glumes and awns

diagnostic_features.value: Bright yellow elongated pustules arranged in conspicuous linear rows (stripes) on leaves, releasing yellow-orange masses of urediniospores when mature. A single infection can produce a stripe the full length of the leaf. In some varieties, long, narrow yellow stripes develop on leaves.
diagnostic_features.quote: small, bright yellow, elongated uredial pustules arranged in conspicuous rows on the leaves, leaf sheaths, glumes and awns. Mature pustules will break open and release yellow-orange masses of urediniospores. In some varieties, long, narrow yellow stripes will develop on leaves.

look_alikes.quote: Stripe rust urediniospores probably are less tolerant of environmental extremes then either leaf or stem rust of wheat.

conflicts.note: USDA ARS lists species-level name without forma specialis; UGA extension specifies f. sp. tritici which is standard for wheat stripe rust.

pathogen_scientific_name.quote: It is caused by the fungus Ustilago tritici .

type_of_disease.quote: It is caused by the fungus Ustilago tritici .

affected_parts.quote: yellowish leaf streaks and stiff, dark green leaves. Affected plants head out early, producing sterile heads with clumped, sooty olive-black spores in place of healthy glumes and kernels.

summary.value: Affected plants head early, producing sterile heads with clumped, sooty olive-black spores replacing healthy glumes and kernels. Prior to heading, mild symptoms include yellowish leaf streaks and stiff, dark green leaves.
summary.quote: Mild symptoms may be present prior to heading, including yellowish leaf streaks and stiff, dark green leaves. Affected plants head out early, producing sterile heads with clumped, sooty olive-black spores in place of healthy glumes and kernels.

diagnostic_features.value: Sterile heads with sooty olive-black spores in place of glumes and kernels; after spore dispersal, only a bare rachis remains with a few fragments of glumes or awns. Loose smut spores will NOT have a fishy odor.
diagnostic_features.quote: Affected plants head out early, producing sterile heads with clumped, sooty olive-black spores in place of healthy glumes and kernels. Spores are not enclosed by the seed coat, so are quickly dispersed by rain or wind after emergence. After spores disperse, only a bare rachis remains with a few fragments of glumes or awns. Loose smut spores will NOT have a fishy odor.

pathogen_scientific_name.quote: Powdery mildew, caused by Blumeria graminis f. sp. tritici

type_of_disease.quote: Blumeria graminis f. sp. tritici (syn. Erysiphe graminis) is an obligate, host specific fungus that attacks wheat exclusively

affected_parts.quote: Powdery mildew is characterized by a powdery white to gray fungal growth on leaves, stems and heads

summary.value: Powdery white to gray fungal growth on upper leaf surfaces and stems, with fluffy white pustules first appearing on lowest leaves, later changing to grey-brown color. Yellow leaf tissue develops on the opposite side of the mold growth. Small black fruiting bodies (cleistothecia) develop in older grey colonies as plants mature.
summary.quote: Powdery mildew is characterized by a powdery white to gray fungal growth on leaves, stems and heads ( Fig. 1 ). The fluffy white pustules are first detected on the lowest leaves of plants in early- to mid-April. As the plant matures, the white powdery growth changes to a grey-brown color.

diagnostic_features.value: White to gray cottony patches on upper leaf surfaces producing large quantities of small asexual conidia (oidia) in long chains; yellow leaf tissue on the opposite side of the mold growth turning tan or brown; distinct round black dots (cleistothecia) within older grey colonies of powdery mildew.
diagnostic_features.quote: Powdery mildew produces a white to gray cottony fungal growth on the upper leaf surface. The white powdery patches or pustules produce large quantities of small asexual conidia (also called oidia) in long chains, which are easily dislodged by wind or rain. Small, black fungal fruiting bodies (cleistothecia) may be seen immersed in the gray fungal tissue later in the season. Usually field symptoms are conspicuous and unique enough that visual inspection will suffice for a rapid identification.

conflicts.alternative_value: Foliar, Whole plant (any above-ground plant part)
conflicts.note: OSU lists leaves, stems, and heads; UGA states the disease may occur on any above-ground plant part but is most prevalent on upper surface of lower leaves.

pathogen_scientific_name.quote: It is caused by Pythium spp. and Globisporangium spp.

type_of_disease.quote: It is caused by Pythium spp. and Globisporangium spp.

affected_parts.quote: Infected roots are shorter, have few root hairs, and are necrotic. Symptoms include stunting, yellowing, tiller reduction, and poor stand.

summary.value: Plants show stunting, yellowing, tiller reduction, and poor stand. Infected roots are shorter, have few root hairs, and are necrotic, with the outer root cortex falling off easily.
summary.quote: Symptoms include stunting, yellowing, tiller reduction, and poor stand. Infected roots are shorter, have few root hairs, and are necrotic. The outer layer of the root (the cortex) falls off easily.

diagnostic_features.value: The outer layer of the root (the cortex) falls off easily on infected plants, and roots are shorter with few root hairs.
diagnostic_features.quote: The outer layer of the root (the cortex) of Pythium -infected plants falls off easily.

pathogen_scientific_name.quote: The wheat streak mosaic virus (WSMV) is a member of the Potyviridae family of viruses.

type_of_disease.quote: The wheat streak mosaic virus (WSMV) is a member of the Potyviridae family of viruses.

affected_parts.quote: Leaves of infected plants show a yellowed mosaic pattern of parallel discontinuous streaks. ... Plants infected before early tillering are stunted, discolored and rosetted.

summary.value: Leaves show a yellowed mosaic pattern of parallel discontinuous streaks that progress to mottled yellow; plants become stunted, discolored, and rosetted.
summary.quote: Leaves of infected plants show a yellowed mosaic pattern of parallel discontinuous streaks. As symptoms, progress the leaves become mottled yellow. Plants infected before early tillering are stunted, discolored and rosetted.

diagnostic_features.value: Streaked mosaic pattern on leaves and rosette appearance of plants; mite-infested leaves have edges rolled inward toward the mid-rib, and new leaf tips trapped in rolled leaves form loops.
diagnostic_features.quote: The streaked mosaic pattern on leaves and the rosette appearance of plants are good field diagnostic symptoms. Mite-infested leaves tend to have their edges rolled inward toward the mid-rib. On a young plant the tip of a new leaf often is trapped in the rolled leaf immediately below it so that the developing leaf is curled black on itself, forming a loop.

pathogen_scientific_name.quote: It is caused by Rhizoctonia solani and R. oryzae.

type_of_disease.quote: Fungicide seed treatments can be used for early season protection against Rhizoctonia root rot.

affected_parts.quote: The pathogen "prunes" roots by girdling them, reducing root mass and capacity to transport water and nutrients to aboveground plant tissue.

summary.value: Field symptoms include bare patches or areas of uneven plant height. Severe infection causes plants to be stunted, appear drought stressed or nutrient deprived, and may result in premature plant death.
summary.quote: Field symptoms include bare patches or areas of uneven plant height. Severe infection causes plants to be stunted, appear drought stressed or nutrient deprived, and may result in premature plant death.

diagnostic_features.value: Roots develop characteristically fine, sharp-looking, red-brown points known as spear tip. Girdling can also make roots look pinched or constricted.
diagnostic_features.quote: Roots develop characteristically fine, sharp-looking, red-brown points known as spear tip. Girdling can also make roots look pinched or constricted.

look_alikes.quote: Severe infection causes plants to be stunted, appear drought stressed or nutrient deprived

pathogen_scientific_name.quote: is caused by Zymoseptoria tritici

type_of_disease.quote: The fungus overwinters on seed, residue, and overwintering cereals.

affected_parts.quote: often occurring alongside other foliar diseases ... The fungus overwinters on seed, residue, and overwintering cereals.

summary.value: Elliptical, tan-brown lesions that often have yellowish halos first appear on seedling leaves. Lesion centers die and dark fruiting bodies are produced, giving the lesion a characteristic speckled appearance. Subsequent lesions on higher leaves generally follow leaf veins, having straight edges and no yellow margins.
summary.quote: Elliptical, tan-brown lesions that often have yellowish halos first appear on seedling leaves. Lesion centers die and dark fruiting bodies are produced, giving the lesion a characteristic speckled appearance. Subsequent lesions on higher leaves generally follow leaf veins, having straight edges and no yellow margins.

diagnostic_features.value: Lesions generally do not have pronounced chlorotic halos like Stagonospora leaf and glume blotch and tan spot; lesions are more elongated with rougher edges. When humid, a translucent, curling thread of whitish ooze may appear from fruiting bodies.
diagnostic_features.quote: Septoria tritici blotch lesions generally do not have pronounced chlorotic halos like Stagonospora leaf and glume blotch and tan spot, and lesions are more elongated with rougher edges. When humid, a translucent, curling thread of whitish ooze may appear from fruiting bodies.

look_alikes.quote: Septoria tritici blotch lesions generally do not have pronounced chlorotic halos like Stagonospora leaf and glume blotch and tan spot

pathogen_scientific_name.quote: Scientific Name: Puccinia triticina (= P. recondita Roberge ex Desmaz. f. sp. tritici .)

type_of_disease.quote: Grain shrivels and nutrients produced primarily in the flag leaf are used by the fungus rather than transported to the grain.

affected_parts.quote: Uredinia normally appear on the upper leaf surface, but with severe epidemics sheath infections can occur.

summary.value: Brown, generally circular uredinia appearing on the upper leaf surface that seldom penetrate through the leaf; with severe epidemics sheath infections can occur.
summary.quote: Uredinia are brown in color and generally circular in shape. Uredinia seldom penetrate through the leaf.

diagnostic_features.value: Brown, circular uredinia on upper leaf surface that seldom penetrate through the leaf; pustules are orange to brown, medium-size and round to slightly elongated, scattered randomly on leaf surface (not in stripes), developing at warmer temperatures (64-77°F).
diagnostic_features.quote: Uredinia normally appear on the upper leaf surface, but with severe epidemics sheath infections can occur. Uredinia are brown in color and generally circular in shape. Uredinia seldom penetrate through the leaf.

look_alikes.quote: Stripe Rust Leaf Rust Stem Rust

conflicts.canonical_value: Brown, generally circular uredinia appearing on the upper leaf surface (USDA Cereal Disease Lab)
conflicts.alternative_value: Orange to brown pustules scattered randomly on leaf surface, round to slightly elongated, medium-sized (Crop Protection Network)

pathogen_scientific_name.quote: Tan spot is caused by Pyrenophora tritici-repentis and is also called yellow leaf spot.

type_of_disease.quote: Infection by the fungus that causes tan spot can occur anytime during the growing season

affected_parts.quote: initially appears as small, brown spots on leaves. ... When infected, kernels may develop a red, dirty appearance known as red smudge.

summary.value: Small tan to brown lens or diamond-shaped spots on leaves that are elliptical to elongate with a dark brown center and yellow border; lesions coalesce into larger irregular dead tissue areas. Kernels may develop a red, dirty appearance known as red smudge.
summary.quote: On leaves, the disease first appears as small, tan to brown lens or diamond-shaped spots. Characteristic symptoms are elliptical to elongate spots that are tan colored, have a dark brown spot near the center and are surrounded by a yellow border. As the lesions increase in size they tend to coalesce, producing larger, irregular areas of dead tissue.

diagnostic_features.value: Elliptical to elongate tan-colored spots with a dark brown spot near the center surrounded by a yellow border; a pinhead-size black spot may be present at the infection site; pseudothecia on stubble feel like coarse sandpaper. The yellow halo distinguishes it from Septoria tritici blotch, and lesions are more angular than Stagonospora leaf blotch.
diagnostic_features.quote: Characteristic symptoms are elliptical to elongate spots that are tan colored, have a dark brown spot near the center and are surrounded by a yellow border. ... pseudothecia are visible on the stubble that remains after harvest and are diagnostic of tan spot. They feel like coarse sandpaper to the touch.

look_alikes.quote: Tan spot lesions have a yellow halo, unlike Septoria tritici blotch, and are more angular than Stagonospora leaf blotch lesions.
